newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Defeated Bhutto ponders political future.
newsitem.headline: Defeated Bhutto ponders political future.

text.p: Benazir Bhutto, twice elected and twice fired as prime minister of Pakistan, faces an uncertain political future after her humiliation at the polls.

Bhutto, 43, the first woman to lead Islamic Pakistan, retained her own seat in Monday's national and provincial elections, but her Pakistan People's Party (PPP) could manage only 18 seats in the 217-seat National Assembly (lower house).
Her chief rival, businessman Nawaz Sharif, romped home with at least 134 seats for his Pakistan Muslim League (PML).
The PPP was virtually wiped out in the assembly in the populous province of Punjab, gaining a meagre two seats.
It may even be unable to form a provincial government on Bhutto's home turf in Sindh, where the PML could ally with a Karachi-based ethnic party and independents to reach a majority.
Bhutto has charged that the polls were rigged, saying she felt "cheated, not defeated". But she has also promised not to try to topple Sharif's government through popular agitation.

Pakistani commentators say the PPP has no one to blame but itself for its dismal showing at the polls, called after President Farooq Leghari sacked Bhutto's government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
Last week's Supreme Court ruling that Leghari's action had been justified dealt a painful pre-election blow to the PPP.
Karachi's English-language daily Dawn said the PPP's path to rehabilitation lay in "a painstaking effort to regain the party's lost idealism and re-define its political aims".
Despite its stinging losses, the PPP received the second highest vote tally. "Nobody should belittle the significance of the PPP. It has the potential for bouncing back," Dawn said.
Diplomats said Bhutto had sounded a conciliatory note, but could still turn militant under party pressure.

However, PPP leaders might also be tempted to blame their defeat on Bhutto's husband, Asif Ali Zardari, her former investment minister who is now in jail on a charge of conspiring to murder his brother-in-law, Murtaza Bhutto.
Zardari, who denies any wrongdoing, was at the centre of corruption allegations that swirled around Bhutto's rule.
"The imperial lifestyle of the First Couple...amid a sea of poverty could have alienated a sizeable chunk of voters," the Peshawar-based newspaper The Frontier Post said.
No corruption charges have yet been brought against Bhutto or her spouse, but that could change now that a perceived danger that the PPP might boycott the elections is over.
"Will Benazir go down with Zardari? Or will she ditch him at last?" one European diplomat asked.

The PPP was clearly hurt, especially in Sindh province, by the ramifications of Murtaza's killing by Karachi police on September 20. His widow, Lebanese-born Ghinwa Bhutto, took over leadership of her husband's breakaway PPP faction, splitting the PPP vote in many of its heartland constituencies.
But Ghinwa has yet to convince the PPP faithful that she is the rightful heir to the once-potent political legacy of the party's founder, executed prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto.
"It is hard to see anyone else rivalling Benazir in the PPP, unless she leaves the country," the diplomat said.

Bhutto has angrily rejected the notion that she might leave Pakistan and politics as part of a deal to avoid a possible corruption trial involving herself and Zardari. "Pakistan is my home and I am going to live in my home," she said.
Bhutto, a gritty fighter, has been on the ropes before and cannot be counted out in Pakistan's topsy-turvy politics.

Charismatic daughter of Pakistan's first popularly elected leader, she took over the PPP after Zulfikar Ali Bhutto was hanged in 1979 on the orders of former military ruler General Mohammed Zia-ul-Haq, who had toppled him in 1977.

For 11 years Bhutto fought vainly against Zia until he died in a 1988 plane crash. She won elections that year, but then President Ghulam Ishaq Khan sacked her after just 20 months, accusing her of presiding over large-scale corruption.
She clawed her way back to power in the October 1993 election after three years in the political wilderness, only to be sacked a second time by a different president.
